topic: Injury and illness recordkeeping and reporting

notes.front: What is a recordable injury or illness under Part 1904?
notes.back: A work-related, new case that meets one or more of the general recording criteria (or the rules for specific cases).
notes.explanation: Part 1904 sets these three tests; a case that fails any one of them is not entered in the records.
notes.example: Like a match that must be official, new and scored before it goes in the league table.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.4(a), p. 4
notes.evidence: must record each fatality, injury and illness that: (1) Is work-related; and (2) Is a new case; and (3) Meets one or more of the general recording criteria

notes.front: What is first aid, for recordkeeping under Part 1904?
notes.back: Only the treatments on Part 1904’s list, such as cleaning surface wounds or using hot or cold therapy; anything else is medical treatment.
notes.explanation: Part 1904 calls its list complete, and medical treatment beyond first aid makes a case recordable.
notes.example: Like a fixed menu: if a treatment is not printed on it, it is not first aid for the records.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.7(b)(5)(iii), p. 11
notes.evidence: No, this is a complete list of all treatments considered first aid for part 1904 purposes.

notes.front: What is the OSHA 300 Log?
notes.back: The Log of Work-Related Injuries and Illnesses: a one- or two-line entry for each recordable injury or illness.
notes.explanation: The employer also enters information about the business at the top of the log.
notes.example: Like a ship’s log, but each line is a work injury or illness rather than a day at sea.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.29(b)(1), p. 14
notes.evidence: You must enter information about your business at the top of the OSHA 300 Log, enter a one or two line description for each recordable injury or illness

notes.front: What is the OSHA 300A Summary?
notes.back: The Summary of Work-Related Injuries and Illnesses: the year’s OSHA 300 Log information summarised at the end of the year.
notes.explanation: It is the form the employer certifies and posts each year.
notes.example: Like an end-of-year scorecard built from a season’s match reports.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.29(a), p. 14
notes.evidence: the 300–A is the Summary of Work-Related Injuries and Illnesses

notes.front: What is the OSHA 301 Incident Report?
notes.back: The Injury and Illness Incident Report, completed for each recordable injury or illness entered on the OSHA 300 Log.
notes.explanation: The log gives one line per case; the 301 is the form for the case in detail.
notes.example: Like the full accident report form that sits behind a single line in a register.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.29(b)(2), p. 14
notes.evidence: You must complete an OSHA 301 Incident Report form, or an equivalent form, for each recordable injury or illness entered on the OSHA 300 Log.

notes.front: What is the purpose of Part 1904?
notes.back: To require employers to record and report work-related fatalities, injuries and illnesses.
notes.explanation: Everything in Part 1904 serves these two acts: keeping records and reporting to the government.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.0, p. 1
notes.evidence: The purpose of this rule (part 1904) is to require employers to record and report work-related fatalities, injuries, and illnesses.

notes.front: Does recording a work-related injury mean the employer was at fault or that an OSHA rule was broken?
notes.back: No. Recording does not mean fault, a violation, or that the employee is eligible for workers’ compensation.
notes.explanation: Part 1904 says so in a note to its purpose section.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.0 note, p. 1
notes.evidence: does not mean that the employer or employee was at fault, that an OSHA rule has been violated, or that the employee is eligible for workers’ compensation or other benefits

notes.front: Which employers are partially exempt from keeping OSHA injury and illness records because of their size?
notes.back: Companies that had 10 or fewer employees at all times during the last calendar year.
notes.explanation: The exemption falls away if OSHA or the Bureau of Labor Statistics tells the company in writing to keep records.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.1(a)(1), p. 2
notes.evidence: If your company had 10 or fewer employees at all times during the last calendar year, you do not need to keep OSHA injury and illness records

notes.front: Must a partially exempt small employer still report a work-related fatality or amputation to OSHA?
notes.back: Yes. All employers covered by the OSH Act must report these events.
notes.explanation: The partial exemption covers keeping records, not the reporting duty in section 1904.39.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.1(a)(1), p. 2
notes.evidence: all employers covered by the OSH Act must report to OSHA any work-related incident that results in a fatality, the in-patient hospitalization of one or more employees, an employee amputation, or an employee loss of an eye

notes.front: When must an employer consider an injury or illness work-related?
notes.back: When an event or exposure in the work environment caused or contributed to it, or significantly aggravated a pre-existing condition.
notes.explanation: Part 1904 presumes work-relatedness for events or exposures in the work environment unless a listed exception applies.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.5(a), p. 5
notes.evidence: if an event or exposure in the work environment either caused or contributed to the resulting condition or significantly aggravated a pre-existing injury or illness

notes.front: What are two of the outcomes that make a work-related injury or illness meet the general recording criteria?
notes.back: Any two of: death; days away from work; restricted work or job transfer; medical treatment beyond first aid; loss of consciousness.
notes.explanation: A significant diagnosed injury or illness also qualifies, even without any of these outcomes.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.7(a), p. 8
notes.evidence: if it results in any of the following: death, days away from work, restricted work or transfer to another job, medical treatment beyond first aid, or loss of consciousness

notes.front: What are two work-related conditions that must always be recorded once a physician or other licensed health care professional diagnoses them?
notes.back: Any two of: cancer; chronic irreversible disease; a fractured or cracked bone; a punctured eardrum.
notes.explanation: These count as significant diagnosed cases, recorded even without days away, restriction or treatment.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.7(b), p. 12
notes.evidence: Work-related cases involving cancer, chronic irreversible disease, a fractured or cracked bone, or a punctured eardrum must always be recorded under the general criteria at the time of diagnosis

notes.front: Besides first aid, what two things does Part 1904 exclude from “medical treatment”?
notes.back: Visits to a health care professional solely for observation or counselling; and diagnostic procedures such as x-rays and blood tests.
notes.explanation: Because these are not medical treatment, they do not on their own make a case recordable.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.7(b)(5)(i), p. 11
notes.evidence: medical treatment does not include: (A) Visits to a physician or other licensed health care professional solely for observation or counseling; (B) The conduct of diagnostic procedures, such as x-rays and blood tests

notes.front: Is giving a tetanus immunisation first aid or medical treatment for recordkeeping?
notes.back: First aid. Other immunisations, such as hepatitis B or rabies vaccine, are medical treatment.
notes.explanation: Part 1904’s list names tetanus alone and puts other immunisations outside it.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.7(b)(5)(ii)(B), p. 11
notes.evidence: Administering tetanus immunizations (other immunizations, such as Hepatitis B vaccine or rabies vaccine, are considered medical treatment)

notes.front: Which wound closures count as first aid, and which as medical treatment?
notes.back: Butterfly bandages and adhesive closure strips are first aid; sutures, staples and similar devices are medical treatment.
notes.explanation: Part 1904 lists ordinary wound coverings and butterfly bandages as first aid, and names other closing devices as treatment.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.7(b)(5)(ii)(D), p. 11
notes.evidence: or using butterfly bandages or Steri-Strips TM (other wound closing devices such as sutures, staples, etc., are considered medical treatment)

notes.front: When does using a non-prescription medicine count as medical treatment?
notes.back: When a physician or other licensed health care professional recommends it at prescription strength.
notes.explanation: At non-prescription strength the same medicine is first aid.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.7(b)(5)(ii)(A), p. 11
notes.evidence: a recommendation by a physician or other licensed health care professional to use a non-prescription medication at prescription strength is considered medical treatment for recordkeeping purposes

notes.front: When do you start counting days away from work for the OSHA 300 Log?
notes.back: On the day after the injury occurred or the illness began.
notes.explanation: The day of the injury itself is not counted.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.7(b)(3)(i), p. 8
notes.evidence: No, you begin counting days away on the day after the injury occurred or the illness began.

notes.front: How quickly must a recordable injury or illness be entered on the OSHA 300 Log and 301 Incident Report?
notes.back: Within seven calendar days of receiving information that it has occurred.
notes.explanation: The clock runs from when the employer receives the information, not from the date of injury.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.29(b)(3), p. 15
notes.evidence: within seven (7) calendar days of receiving information that a recordable injury or illness has occurred

notes.front: At the end of each calendar year, what must the employer do with the OSHA 300 Log before posting?
notes.back: Review it for completeness and accuracy; create an annual summary; certify the summary.
notes.explanation: Posting the summary is the fourth step Part 1904 lists.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.32(a), p. 17
notes.evidence: (1) Review the OSHA 300 Log to verify that the entries are complete and accurate, and correct any deficiencies identified; (2) Create an annual summary of injuries and illnesses recorded on the OSHA 300 Log; (3) Certify the summary; and (4) Post the annual summary.

notes.front: Who must certify the annual summary?
notes.back: A company executive, such as an officer of the corporation or the highest ranking company official working at the establishment.
notes.explanation: The executive certifies having examined the log and reasonably believing the summary correct and complete.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.32(b)(3), p. 17
notes.evidence: A company executive must certify that he or she has examined the OSHA 300 Log and that he or she reasonably believes

notes.front: Between which dates must the annual summary be posted?
notes.back: From no later than 1 February of the following year until 30 April.
notes.explanation: The summary covers the previous calendar year and stays up for three months.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.32(b)(6), p. 17
notes.evidence: You must post the summary no later than February 1 of the year following the year covered by the records and keep the posting in place until April 30.

notes.front: How long must the OSHA 300 Log, annual summary and 301 forms be kept?
notes.back: Five years following the end of the calendar year that the records cover.
notes.explanation: During that period the stored logs must be updated for newly discovered cases and changes in classification.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.33(a), p. 17
notes.evidence: Incident Report forms for five (5) years following the end of the calendar year that these records cover

notes.front: If an employee asks for a copy of the OSHA 300 Log, how quickly must the employer provide it?
notes.back: By the end of the next business day.
notes.explanation: Employees, former employees, their personal representatives and authorised employee representatives all have a right of access.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.35(b)(2), p. 18
notes.evidence: you must give the requester a copy of the relevant OSHA 300 Log(s) by the end of the next business day

notes.front: What does Part 1904 forbid an employer to do to an employee who reports a work-related injury?
notes.back: Discharge or in any manner discriminate against the employee.
notes.explanation: Part 1904 also requires a reporting procedure that would not deter a reasonable employee from reporting.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.35(b)(1)(iv), p. 18
notes.evidence: You must not discharge or in any manner discriminate against any employee for reporting a work-related injury or illness.

notes.front: Within how many hours must an employer report a work-related fatality to OSHA?
notes.back: Eight hours after the death.
notes.explanation: The duty applies when the death results from a work-related incident.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.39(a)(1), p. 21
notes.evidence: Within eight (8) hours after the death of any employee as a result of a work-related incident, you must report the fatality

notes.front: Which three work-related events must be reported to OSHA within 24 hours?
notes.back: In-patient hospitalisation of one or more employees; an amputation; loss of an eye.
notes.explanation: These carry a longer window than a fatality, which must be reported within eight hours.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.39(a)(2), p. 21
notes.evidence: Within twenty-four (24) hours after the in-patient hospitalization of one or more employees or an employee’s amputation or an employee’s loss of an eye

notes.front: A worker dies of his injuries 40 days after a work-related incident. Must the death be reported to OSHA?
notes.back: No, a fatality is reported only if it occurs within 30 days of the incident; it must still be recorded.
notes.explanation: For hospitalisation, amputation or loss of an eye, the event must occur within 24 hours of the incident to be reportable.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.39(b), p. 22
notes.evidence: You must only report a fatality to OSHA if the fatality occurs within thirty (30) days of the work-related incident.

notes.front: By which methods may an employer report a fatality or serious injury to OSHA?
notes.back: By telephone or in person to the nearest Area Office; by OSHA’s toll-free number; or electronically through OSHA’s website.
notes.explanation: If the Area Office is closed, only the toll-free number or the website will do: no answering machine, fax or email.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.39(a)(3), p. 21
notes.evidence: By telephone or in person to the OSHA Area Office that is nearest to the site of the incident.

notes.front: A labourer cuts his hand; the clinic closes it with three sutures and he returns to work the same shift. Is the case recordable?
notes.back: C: yes, sutures are medical treatment beyond first aid.
notes.choices:
A) No, he lost no time
B) No, clinic visits are first aid
C) Yes, sutures are medical treatment beyond first aid
D) Only if he is hospitalised
notes.choicesExplained: A: days away are only one criterion. B: only listed treatments are first aid. D: hospitalisation affects reporting, not whether a case is recorded.
notes.explanation: Medical treatment beyond first aid is itself one of the general recording criteria.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.7(b)(5)(ii)(D), p. 11
notes.evidence: other wound closing devices such as sutures, staples, etc., are considered medical treatment

notes.front: A roofing firm had 8 employees all last year. It has had no written request from OSHA or the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Must it keep an OSHA 300 Log?
notes.back: B: no, it is partially exempt.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, all construction firms must
B) No, it is partially exempt
C) Yes, but only the 301 forms
D) Only if it has an accident
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D: the exemption for 10 or fewer employees at all times covers keeping the records, whatever the industry or events.
notes.explanation: It must still report any fatality, in-patient hospitalisation, amputation or loss of an eye.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.1(a)(1), p. 2
notes.evidence: If your company had 10 or fewer employees at all times during the last calendar year, you do not need to keep OSHA injury and illness records

notes.front: At 9 a.m. a worker loses a fingertip in a saw. The Area Office is closed for a holiday. What must the employer do?
notes.back: D: report it within 24 hours by the toll-free number or OSHA’s website.
notes.choices:
A) Report it within 8 hours by fax
B) Wait until the Area Office reopens
C) Record it only; amputations need no report
D) Report it within 24 hours by the toll-free number or OSHA’s website
notes.choicesExplained: A: 8 hours is for fatalities, and fax is not accepted. C: amputations are reportable. B: when the office is closed the other two methods must be used.
notes.explanation: An amputation is the traumatic loss of a limb or other external body part.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.39(b)(1), p. 21
notes.evidence: if the Area Office is closed, you must report the fatality, in-patient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye using either the 800 number or the reporting application

notes.front: A worker is killed in a fall at 2 p.m. By when must the employer report the death to OSHA?
notes.back: D: by 10 p.m. the same day.
notes.choices:
A) At the next annual summary
B) By 2 p.m. the next day
C) Within 7 calendar days
D) By 10 p.m. the same day
notes.choicesExplained: B is the 24-hour window for hospitalisations and amputations. C is the deadline for recording on the log. A: the summary is not a report.
notes.explanation: Eight hours after 2 p.m. is 10 p.m.; the death must also be recorded.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.39(a)(1), p. 21
notes.evidence: Within eight (8) hours after the death of any employee as a result of a work-related incident

notes.front: A site manager learns on Monday 4 March that a worker broke a wrist at work. By what date must the case be on the OSHA 300 Log?
notes.back: B: by Monday 11 March.
notes.choices:
A) By the next day
B) By Monday 11 March
C) By 1 February next year
D) Only if the worker takes days off
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule allows seven calendar days. C is the summary posting date. D: a fractured bone is always recordable when diagnosed.
notes.explanation: Seven calendar days from receiving the information lands on 11 March.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.29(b)(3), p. 15
notes.evidence: within seven (7) calendar days of receiving information that a recordable injury or illness has occurred

notes.front: It is 15 March 2027. Which injury summary should be on the site notice board, and until when?
notes.back: A: the 2026 summary, until 30 April 2027.
notes.choices:
A) The 2026 summary, until 30 April 2027
B) None; posting ended on 1 March
C) The 2027 summary so far, until year-end
D) The 2026 summary, until 31 December 2027
notes.choicesExplained: B: the posting runs to 30 April. C: the summary covers the previous year. D: the posting ends on 30 April.
notes.explanation: The summary for a year is posted by 1 February of the next year, so 2026’s is up in spring 2027.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.32(b)(6), p. 17
notes.evidence: You must post the summary no later than February 1 of the year following the year covered by the records and keep the posting in place until April 30.

notes.front: A contractor wants to shred its 2021 OSHA 300 Log. What is the earliest year it may lawfully do so?
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C fall inside the five years that run from the end of 2021, that is, to the end of 2026.
notes.explanation: Five years after 31 December 2021 is the end of 2026, so disposal can come in 2027.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.33(a), p. 17
notes.evidence: for five (5) years following the end of the calendar year that these records cover

notes.front: A foreman tells his crew that anyone who reports an injury will lose their overtime. What does Part 1904 say about this?
notes.back: B: forbidden; it discriminates against employees for reporting.
notes.choices:
A) Allowed, if injuries are still recorded
B) Forbidden: it discriminates against employees for reporting
C) Allowed for minor injuries
D) Allowed during the first 90 days of employment
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D: Part 1904 forbids discrimination in any manner for reporting, with no exception.
notes.explanation: A procedure that would deter a reasonable employee from reporting is also not reasonable under Part 1904.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.35(b)(1)(i), p. 18
notes.evidence: A procedure is not reasonable if it would deter or discourage a reasonable employee from accurately reporting a workplace injury or illness

notes.front: How does the OSHA 300 Log differ from the OSHA 301 Incident Report?
notes.back: The log has one or two lines per case for the whole establishment; the 301 is a separate report for each case.
notes.explanation: Part 1904 names the three forms together: 300 Log, 300–A Summary and 301 Incident Report.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.29(a), p. 14
notes.evidence: The OSHA 300 form is called the Log of Work-Related Injuries and Illnesses, the 300–A is the Summary of Work-Related Injuries and Illnesses, and the OSHA 301 form is called the Injury and Illness Incident Report.

notes.front: What is the difference between recording and reporting under Part 1904?
notes.back: Recording means entering cases in the employer’s own forms; reporting means telling OSHA about deaths and severe injuries within hours.
notes.explanation: A reportable event must also be recorded if the employer keeps records.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1904 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1904.39(b), p. 21
notes.evidence: However, the fatality, in-patient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye must be recorded on your OSHA injury and illness records, if you are required to keep such records.
